I think it must be pretty hard to buy gifts for folks who love RPGs if you yourself are not familiar with them, because as I’ve discovered today while perusing the internet for ideas, most searches for RPG-themed gifts get you into the territory of tabletop RPGs rather than video game RPGs. Don’t get me wrong, I love a good TTRPG, but sometimes that’s not what you’re looking for exactly.

This is a guide to shopping for the RPG-lover in your life, someone who you know really likes a good role-playing video game with stats that go up as you level up, a nice big fantasy world of some sort, stuff you can equip to make yourself stronger, probably a party of heroes adventuring together, and possibly some interesting moments where you can make choices that influence what happens next. There are a lot of games that fall into this category, and the RPG-lover in your life may or may not like some or all of these. So as with all gifts, try to get to know the person you’re gifting something to just a little and make sure you’re getting, say, a game for a system they actually own, or a piece of merchandise for one they already played and liked.

It has been revealed that with that in mind, here you are! 12 ideas!

Don’t worry, this list won’t be all straight-up games, but I did want to sprinkle a few recent releases in here to hopefully give you some options of newer games to gift that might broaden your giftee’s horizons. Trails in the Sky 1st ChapterÂ is a remake, released last year, of the original Trails in the Sky, which is the start of an excellent RPG that’s nonetheless (I think) overlooked by a lot of general RPG fans. The remake itself looks really nice, and the music is incredible. If you know someone who already has 1st Chapter in their library, 2nd Chapter came out this year too!

It has been revealed that I’m not a huge collector of video game-themed merchandise, especially stuff that’s really obviously “gamer”, you know? But I have to admit these towels get me every time. It’s a genuinely funny play on a death screen from an iconic RPG series that anyone who’s touched a Souls game will probably find at least somewhat amusing.

The Adventures of Elliot is another release from this year, and while it’s not my personal favorite RPG, it’s got a lot going for it and a ton of RPG fans seemed to really dig it. Not a traditional turn-based RPG, this game instead has a singular main character, Elliot, who can switch between several different weapon types in action combat to dispatch monsters. It’s got that gorgeous HD-2D look that Square Enix has been using to marry a retro feel with modern visuals, and a pretty interesting story involving time travel to see the same world across multiple eras.

In a recent development, I’ve been seeing these little music boxes around for a bunch of different games, and I think they’re a really neat idea. But for an RPG fan, the absolute safest and best bet for a theme they’ll recognize is one from Final Fantasy. FF7 has several different ones, including both Tifa and Aerith’s themes, and there are more on the Square Enix store if you want to check that out or look for a music box for a specific game.

Industry observers note that I tried to recommend several different kinds of RPGs on this list, depending on what the RPG gamer in your life most often plays. Beast of Reincarnation is a new game from the Pokemon developers, out this year, but it’s a far cry from what Pokemon is. Instead of capturing monsters, you and a single creature partner fight off blight-diseased enemies and explore a post-apocalyptic world using nature-based powers. It’s a game about humans, nature, and human nature, and might appeal especially to fans of the NieR games on aesthetic alone.

According to recent reports, hell yeah I’m recommending a dang notebook and pen. Who doesn’t love these? Seriously. As an RPG lover I frequently end up taking notes while playing games, either to solve puzzles, remember who the heck characters with fancy names are, or just doodling. And there are so many very cool notebooks and pens out there! You can go two directions with this. You can get something that has a very fantastical outward appearance, like this journal, or you could get a really nice-quality, plain notebook (the paper quality on this one is excellent and feels good to write on). For pens, you could get some colorful gel pens (everyone loves colors) or get a little fancy with it and introduce them to the world of fountain pens. This fountain pen is inexpensive and totally fineâif they really get into them, they may want to upgrade on a future holiday, but keep it simple for now.

In a recent development, this is coming out on December 3, so in just a few days: it’s Xenoblade 3 on Switch 2! Xenoblade 3 is already an excellent game, its Switch 2 version will include a upcoming recruitable character and a quest to obtain them, a new battle mode, newly-voiced event scenes, and it’s in 4K with a glorious 60fps. Check in first to see if the person already has this game on Switch, though, as the upgrade pack by itself to the Switch 2 edition is admittedly a bit cheaper.

Sources indicate that I love video game cookbooks. The ones by author Chelsea Monroe-Cassel are responsible for teaching me to cook in the first place! My two favorites of hers are the World of Warcraft Official Cookbook (and its sequel, Newly introduced Flavors of Azeroth) and The Elder Scrolls Cookbook. All three are fun, easy to follow for novice cooks, and the recipes you end up with are both tasty and unique, often introducing me to ingredients I had never used before. The photography is also lovely, so even if your giftee doesn’t cook, they make a nice collector’s item for fans of the games. If neither of these games appeal, there’s a whole host of other video game cookbooks out there to choose from.

I dunno, I just wish someone would buy this for me. It’s cute and, if you like Undertale, actually extremely funny. Trust me, you’ll know if the RPG fan in your life likes Undertale.

I’m genuinely not sure what it is, but every time I go to Japan for work, someone asks me to get them one of these Dragon Quest slimes. They come in several different versions at varying prices, so take your pick if you know someone who loves Dragon Quest.

Recent findings suggest that oh my God. These…are hilarious. For those who loved last year’s hit RPG Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, these slippers are sure to get a laugh when unwrapped. They’re a hilarious tribute to a character who was obsessed with collecting monster feet, and they look extremely comfy to boot. Possibly a good gift even if someone didn’t play Expedition 33 on sheer utility.

Yeah, really. I’m personally ambivalent about getting gift cards, as if that’s all you’re getting someone it can seem a tad thoughtless. But if you’re shopping for a kid who’s getting multiple things, or a secret Santa you don’t know well, this can be an okay choice. A Steam gift card will go over well with almost anyone who plays games on their PC because they can buy whatever RPG has been on their wishlist (though you can also just peek at their wishlist and buy one for them). You can also get cards for the digital storefronts on PlayStation,Â Xbox, or Nintendo consoles for those that own them. Take your pick.

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level. Some are saying it's too easy. Rockstar boss Rob Nelson has now entered the conversation, telling Destructoid that Rockstar's data demonstrated that GTA 4 was "a little too punishing in places" and GTA 5 was "perhaps too easy." So with GTA 6, the team trying to "land somewhere in the middle." GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition. That stated, players can adjust things like aiming controls, while players can unlock cheat codes to make the game easier or harder. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dJDf76QVv70 Design producer Scott Mitchell, meanwhile, said the fail states in GTA 6 were designed to feel "appropriate." “We wanted to keep things open and not limit the players’ use of mechanics, such as stealth, but we did also want to make sure we retained the cinematic, high production value, explosive sequences that we’re known for, and people expect. It feels like we’ve managed to strike a good balance," he explained. Also in the interview, Nelson said figuring out the difficulty level for GTA 6 is itself challenging because the designers themselves know enemy positions better than anyone after playing and testing the game so much. "There’s a real process in unpicking some of that to create an experience most players will be able to enjoy, rather than endure," Nelson said. "The game is so significant, and has such a wide range of content that we can really lean into that, making certain open-world content--compounds and fronts for example---more difficult, to give players seeking a challenge something to sink their teeth into as well.” GTA 6 launched on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In its latest upgrade on deprecated features in Windows, Microsoft casually mentioned that "Telnet Client is deprecated and will be removed from Windows in a future release.".
  • Recent findings suggest that this may not mean much to you if you didn't do a lot of computer networking in the 1990s or earlier, but the text-based protocol for remotely opening command-line interfaces was a workhorse we used for a bunch of things.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its latest upgrade on deprecated features in Windows, Microsoft casually mentioned that "Telnet Client is deprecated and will be removed from Windows in a future release.".

Recent findings suggest that this may not mean much to you if you didn't do a lot of computer networking in the 1990s or earlier, but the text-based protocol for remotely opening command-line interfaces was a workhorse we used for a bunch of things. It's how antique university lab computers that didn't even have Netscape Navigator installed connected to the internet, how I played text-based online games like the Discworld MUD back in the day, and how we used to connect to our routers.

According to recent reports, by default, Telnet didn't encrypt all the data it was swapping back and forth between computers, which is why it's since been replaced by tools like SSH and PowerShell. So it's not a surprise that it's being deprecated, and honestly I'm impressed that it outlived both WordPad and Cortana.

A Windows feature being deprecated means that it won't be in active development and is a candidate for removal in a future revision, so Telnet isn't being 86ed immediately. If you're still using it to test network connections because that's what you're used to then carry on as you were, but get ready to grumble and switch over to PowerShell when Microsoft finally does pull the plug.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and was already mapping out the TV adaptation in her head.

Recent findings suggest that the plot heavily involved a Texas abortion clinic, and the state had just passed SB 8, one of the country’s most restrictive abortion bills until Roe v. Wade was overturned the following year. As she contemplated bringing The Hunting Wives to life, Cutter saw the political stakes come into focus as well.

“I started thinking about the ‘red state, blue state’ of it,” she tells Vanity Fair ahead of the show’s season two premiere on Thursday. “What if…we really play this culture war?”.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes,” says showrunner Rebecca Cutter. “I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.”.

Recent findings suggest that the result was one of Netflix’s biggest breakout hits in recent years, sent up in a Saturday Night Live sketch as the “straight but lesbian, horny Republican murder drama.” As a show, Hunting Wives amps up the noirish aspects of the suspense thriller written by May Cobb, a native of the East Texas Piney Woods, and adds a heaping dose of MAGA-adjacent camp. Cutter finishes the mix with plenty of sex scenes, particularly between Malin Akerman’s Margo, a femme fatale partly inspired by Melania Trump who is married to a Republican gubernatorial hopeful, and Brittany Snow’s Sophie, a liberal do-gooder who, like Cutter, arrives in town from a blue corner of Massachusetts. (Cutter was raised in Cambridge and graduated from Wesleyan University, the Connecticut liberal arts college known for its progressive politics and pipeline to Hollywood.).

Hunting Wives executive producer Erwin Stoff told Cutter he’d pay for her to go to Texas to meet Cobb and breathe the Piney Woods air herself. She met Cobb’s father and her best friend from high school. She shot skeet with the women—she even got it in three, just as Sophie does in the first season. At a high-end Dallas shopping area where the likes of Gucci can be found, Cutter got a better sense of the hair, clothes, and bodies of her eventual characters. “I understand the notion that Sophie could be amused and entertained and intrigued by these women,” Cutter notes, “and eventually seduced.”.

According to recent reports, cutter thinks of the show primarily in terms of its tonal mash-up: “I think we managed to wrangle it into one piece of art,” she says, “but there’s comedy, there’s violence, there’s noir, there’s soap, there’s earnest emotion.” To the extent that she assigned any political beliefs to the rich white women of Cobb’s novel, it was in the spirit of grounding her characters in the specifics of their world. Still, as we speak, Cutter decides “to get real with it.”.

Cutter on set. She describes Sophie, a fellow native of blue Massachusetts, as a surrogate for her own awakening to MAGA Texas.

In a recent development, “The whole thing was a little bit of a parable, in my mind, of how you could fall for someone like [Donald] Trump,” she admits. “Sophie has her principles, but they only go so far. They end right where something starts to make her feel good.” Cutter was as curious as anyone else from her educated milieu about the quirkier aspects of Trump, like the Diet Coke button he had installed on the Resolute Desk. How liberating must it feel to embrace a movement so openly untethered from the pieties of politics and taste?

“Not that my show is a deep dive on Trump,” Cutter indicates, “but maybe there is an element that’s sort of looking under the hood.”.

According to recent reports, the twisted love story between Margo and Sophie entangles all of the wealthy, hard-drinking, gun-toting women in their orbit, and its central killing—one of several propelling the show forward, with a third season slated to begin filming this year—stems from an effort to cover up Margo’s abortion as her NRA-loving husband plots his political ascent. (In this proudly oversexed town, he has his own share of affairs.) Hunting Wives is the rare Netflix soap to receive steady coverage from mainstream national outlets; the fascination undoubtedly has something to do with the impression that, like Yellowstone or Morgan Wallen before it, the show unlocks something about MAGA’s cultural staying power. In a Latest York Times guest essay this month that evaluated the post-2024 Hollywood landscape, Sharon Waxman, the editor in chief of The Wrap, wrote, “From Melania on Amazon’s streaming service to The Hunting Wives on Netflix to the ever-expanding Taylor Sheridan universe on Paramount+ to Bari Weiss’s being put in charge of CBS News, the vibe shift was visible on all our screens.”.

Margo and her politically ambitious husband are partners in subterfuge and debauchery.

Cutter states she had no particular agenda nor any “ultra-evil villain plan of how it was going to be received or how it would be culturally relevant.” But Hunting Wives is sprinkled with enough proper nouns—a Peter Thiel mention here, a Walmart reference there—and distinctly modern aesthetics that she can acknowledge its appeal as something of a Rosetta stone for the moment in MAGA femininity. Even in the ostensibly waning days of the movement, the plastic surgery and soaring heels continue to captivate and horrify coastal elites. Cutter says that Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), another of Margo’s lovers, has a bit of Kristi Noem and Marjorie Taylor Greene in her: that “sort of slightly butch, real gun, real ‘back the blue’ [element]…the toughness of those women.”.

The second season of Hunting Wives maintains the slipperiness that keeps the show from veering into moralism; it stands apart from other Trump-era art in its refusal to take sides. “I think I remember, in the pitch, someone saying, ‘But will red-state people like it too?’” Cutter recalls. “I was like, ‘I think so.’” Both Margo and Sophie are awash in their respective red and blue stereotypes, but neither is more admirable than the other. Their sordid union is a testament to the flexibility of both their principles and their preferences. From one vantage, it is, in the end, all about sex.

It has been revealed that “Margo is the symbol of freedom and sexuality and feminine power and empoweredness and selfishness that [Sophie] feels she’s lost,” Cutter notes, adding that Akerman’s comfort in such a role helped drive her liberal use of physical intimacy. “The audience may disagree with me,” she says, but “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes. I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.” Last year, though, when Netflix acquired Hunting Wives, which was initially ordered by Starz in 2023, Cutter had a more practical concern.

“I literally googled,” she recalls, “‘Does Netflix show boobs?’”.

Sources indicate that yet 2023’s Square Enix visual novel Paranormasaight is arguably proof that spoilers may not hurt sales, even for story-driven games. This mystery adventure game limited streamers from sharing just the final chapter online, and lifted this after less than a month. Oushu mentioned that streaming helped raise awareness for the game. âThe people who are going to buy the game will buy it even if all the tricks get revealed in a video,â he claimed.

Industry observers note that it can especially help in long-term sales after a gameâs launch, Oushu argued. Heavier restrictions, he argued, wonât allow players that sense of discovery. It also helped sales for the more recently released sequel: some who watched videos of the first game would go on to play the sequel themselves, without watching streaming content beforehand.

The debate on game streaming has mostly been settled. Today, Twitch is one of the biggest online video platforms, Nintendo lifted restrictions many years ago, and influencers are a key part of promoting almost every modern game released today. But there is still the argument it could hurt smaller and niche titles, and both producers acknowledged the relatively lower prices of their games as factors in their success despite streaming.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quentin Tarantino has returned to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" (why not read our review of the upcoming movie here?). But this time, while Tarantino penned the script, he isn't in the director's chair. Instead, he's handed directing duties over to his pal David Fincher (who is ending his exclusive deal with Netflix with the film). Tarantino might not be behind the camera, but he still has a presence in the film, and it echoes something he did in "Hollywood" as well.

According to recent reports, early in "Cliff Booth," we're introduced to Charlie Peters, a hot-tempered TV star played by Scott Caan. To speed-run us through Charlie's successful career, we're given a little montage of his various roles, and that montage is narrated by none other than Tarantino, whose very recognizable voice provides some humorous details about Charlie's work.

Fans of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" will recall that Tarantino also provided narration in that movie, too. He actually wasn't the only narrator, either, because during one scene, Kurt Russell, who plays a stuntman named Randy in that film, also provides a little narration. As for Tarantino, he also voiced some crucial narration during a pivotal scene in "The Hateful Eight.".

In fact, the filmmaker has a history of popping up in his movies, either via a voice cameo or a physical appearance. He has a pretty significant role in "Reservoir Dogs," makes a memorable cameo in "Pulp Fiction," gets to use an abysmal Australian accent in "Django Unchained," has his voice heard during a movie playing in "Inglourious Basterds" (and also plays a corpse in the film), plays a bartender in "Death Proof," portrays one of the members of the Crazy 88 gang in "Kill Bill," and lends his voice to an answering machine in "Jackie Brown.".

So while "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may not technically be a Quentin Tarantino movie, it still feels like one, right down to the obligatory cameo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that here it was, the big reveal. After years of planning and wrangling, after more than $10 million spent on engineers and lawyers and architects, after all of the rumors and headlines and finger-pointing, the long-awaited presentation was ready to be made.

About 42 seconds after it started, things went off the rails. A “shitshow,” as multiple people would later describe to Vanity Fair the two-and-a-half-hour meeting on the morning of July 29.

The setting was the Cotillion Ballroom, the chandeliered 4,000-square-foot event space at New York’s iconic Pierre Hotel, the site of Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman, where the ceilings are 19 feet high, the curtains are golden, and the windows offer views of Central Park’s southeast corner. Seated at round tables were 40 or so of the people with enough disposable income to call the Pierre home, or at least a home: investor Austin Hearst; Tory Burch, the fashion powerhouse; Lois Chiles, the 1970s-era movie star and model. Joining remotely was Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, who last year spent $4.3 million to buy a second apartment there and, with it, even more shares in the co-op that owns the Pierre.

In came representatives from the Khashoggi Holding Company out of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and the Dorchester Collection, the luxury hotel management firm owned by the Sultan of Brunei. Their proposition was straightforward. Khashoggi wanted to buy the Pierre—the nearly 200-room hotel and all of the apartments too—for $2 billion, less expenses. It was an enormous haul, even for a neighborhood this tony. And it would be all in cash. “The funds are currently available,” a Khashoggi representative promised.

But if the residents with two thirds of the co-op’s shares accepted the offer, everyone would have to move out. Neighbors would be voting, in effect, to force their fellow neighbors from their apartments.

It would be in their best interest, the Dorchester and Khashoggi reps stated. The Pierre was a gem, but a tarnished one after 96 summers and thousands of guests. It didn’t have many of the amenities that come standard these days in a five-star hotel. The façade was already undergoing a $22 million overhaul, and there were deeper, systemic problems to solve. The CEO of the company managing the Pierre publicly complained it was something of a money pit. All of that would change after Khashoggi bought the place, the presenters promised. Dorchester would invest more than $1 billion into the Pierre, giving the landmark building a grand newly introduced entrance on 61st Street, a pool in the basement, and structural renovations throughout.

When it was done, the residents would be first in line to buy apartments at the all-new, all-modern Dorchester-managed Pierre, ready to last another century.

The response in the Cotillion room was instant and not particularly friendly. Some residents had moved in not long ago. Others had spent millions remodeling their apartments. “How are we going to enjoy all the perks of this wonderfully renewed building when we’re forced to sell at a price you determine and we have to buy reconfigured apartments, not our own, at market prices?” asked Tina Beriro, the philanthropist and longtime resident, in a recording of the meeting reviewed by Vanity Fair. Like many of the residents, Beriro, at 85, was only a few years younger than the hotel itself. “Many of us are going to be dead by the time you finish.”.

Christopher Cowdray, Dorchester’s white-haired, Zimbabwe-born president, didn’t have an answer. Nor did he provide much of a response when asked what would happen to the more than 400 people who work at the hotel. “In this case, we are still in discussion at the moment,” Cowdray said, to audible groans.

“Many employees have worked here 30 and 40 years and are just about to hit retirement,” Burch pointed out, per the recording. “I have people in the elevator crying that they feel like their job is on the line.”.

The questions kept coming. For years, shareholders had begged—and even sued—to find out more about the sale. But the long-promised detailed aims for the Pierre’s purchase were still weeks away, adding to the tension in the Cotillion room. (One source, very much in favor of a sale, later called the decision to make an elaborate presentation to the shareholders without those specifics “idiotic.”).

Industry observers note that “Look, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been on the board of the Hearst Corporation for over 25 years. Sat on the boards of many corporations, for profit and not for profit. I have never seen anything like this,” Hearst said, his voice cracking. “This is a serious problem that you have presented to the shareholders, and you guys have done a miserable fucking job.”.

Sources indicate that one of the many lawyers in the room interrupted him, and they started going at it. Cowdray and the other presenters were escorted out. At one point, the wife of Michael Stern, the 88-year-old chairman of the co-op’s board, tried to offer his resignation on his behalf (which he then turned down). Even by the famously hostile standards of Latest York City’s high-end co-ops, this was nasty.

Ironically, the co-op’s biggest shareholder—the resident with the most at stake in the sale financially—didn’t show up. Howard Lutnick was busy in the Oval Office that day with President Donald Trump in his role as US commerce secretary.

Lutnick had bought the Pierre’s 16-room penthouse, its largest apartment, in 2017 for $44 million. If the sale of the Pierre were to go through, Lutnick would get as much as $100 million for the penthouse, even as his neighbors were forced to sell and hundreds of hotel staffers’ jobs were put in jeopardy. Newmark Group—the real estate services firm hired by the Pierre’s board and controlled by Cantor Fitzgerald, the brokerage house previously run by Lutnick—would earn tens of millions more.

Newmark may have a reputation for shepherding big-ticket sales to completion. But in a letter to the Pierre’s board last year, Beriro called the hiring of the Lutnick-linked firm “a blatant conflict of interest,” an allegation sources close to Lutnick and the board deny. One Pierre resident tells me that Lutnick’s involvement is symbolic of a “culture of corruption” that extends from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington to the edges of Central Park in New York. Others imply it is part of a different pattern: the purchase of more and more of America’s most valuable assets by companies and sovereign wealth funds from the Persian Gulf’s petrostates, at times orchestrated by those in and around the second Trump administration. Those shareholders wonder whether Lutnick had personally worked behind the scenes to maneuver the Khashoggi group into place to buy the Pierre, and that speculation spilled onto the pages of The New York Times.

BALL GAMES Guests attend a Valentino party in the Cotillion Ballroom at the Pierre hotel, 1970, New York.

According to recent reports, A source close to Lutnick notes that he formally cut ties with Newmark in early 2025 and adds that, since his move to government, Lutnick’s only involvement in the Pierre sales process has been to respond to media reports like this one. A spokesperson for Sabre Park Avenue LLC, Khashoggi’s American holding organization, tells Vanity Fair in a statement that “any insinuation or implication that the proposal, the transaction or the parties involved engaged in improper or undisclosed conduct is categorically false.”.

I spoke to more than 15 sources and reviewed hundreds of pages of documents related to the Pierre deal, including previously unreported text messages between Lutnick and Khashoggi and a corporate intelligence dossier dropped in my mailbox.

Turns out, the shareholders were right to wonder about Lutnick’s role.

The Pierre for decades was synonymous with Newly introduced York glamour. At the height of their star power, Audrey Hepburn stayed in the hotel’s suites and Elizabeth Taylor kept an apartment there. The restaurant’s original menu was created by Escoffier. Barbara Walters had a reception for her final wedding at the Pierre (about 10 years after she and my grandfather, the Broadway producer Lee Guber, officially split). Yves Saint Laurent owned a two-bedroom on the 38th floor, which was later bought by Valentino cofounder Giancarlo Giammetti, who then sold it to former Bottega Veneta creative director Tomas Maier.

Industry observers note that and yet for 15 years or more, there’s been a growing sense that the Pierre’s best days are behind it, even as the stars continue to use the hotel to get ready for the Met Gala. A 2010 Wall Street Journal article mentions how the Pierre “lost its glory.” By the time Lutnick swooped in to buy the penthouse in 2017, he did so at an $81 million discount off its original asking price.

THE TORY PARTY Fashion designer Tory Burch, in one of the hotel’s elevators, was among the residents opposed to the sale.

Since then, age has continued to take its toll. Scaffolding has surrounded the hotel since at least 2018, according to city records. Exit a multimillion-dollar apartment with a spectacular view of the park and you’re liable to find worn carpets or hallways with the faint odor of mold. Rooms at the Pierre tend to cost much less than they do at the Plaza or the Ritz-Carlton, just around the corner.

In a recent development, over time, a group of shareholders became particularly vexed with Taj Hotels, which had managed the property since 2005. There were complaints of broken elevators, empty concierge desks, and “slipshod maintenance.” Maier, in an October 2023 co-op-wide email, lamented that Taj delayed long-planned renovations to his apartment for months, citing high hotel occupancy. (A Taj spokesperson remarked in a statement those concerns “reflected a specific point in time rather than the overall trajectory of the property.”).

What Maier may not have known—and what the residents I spoke to were unaware of—was that the Pierre’s board had already explored the possibility of replacing Taj. The only way to do that, to break the contract with Taj, was to sell the Pierre. In April 2023, the board drafted a memorandum of understanding with the Maybourne Hotel Group, which is primarily owned by members of the Qatari royal family, to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre. “But there was a condition,” a source familiar with the matter tells me. “Everybody had to move out for two years.” The source adds, “You cannot renovate a 100-year-old building with people living in it, right?”.

Industry observers note that that was a deal killer. So the board decided, in this source’s words, to hire a firm that could broker a “more acceptable” sale. They picked the real estate consultancy Newmark. Lutnick was still chairman of Newmark’s board at that time, though two sources say he had no role in the decision. (The board, through its attorney, declined to comment for this story. But a Newmark spokesperson indicates its “unanimous” selection was “based on the firm’s experience advising on some of Latest York City’s most complex and high-profile real estate transactions.”).

From there, “Newmark went out to find another buyer,” the first source adds. Its fee at the time: $50,000 per month, to be counted against any future commissions in the event of a sale. (Eventually that was bargained down to a flat $30 million.) The board retained the high-profile law firm Fried Frank, which had represented Lutnick’s companies before, to assist Newmark in its search.

LONDON'S CALLING Christopher Cowdray, the Dorchester Collection’s president, was part of the contentious presentation to residents in the Cotillion ballroom at the Pierre.

Since Lutnick’s financial firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, owned a controlling stake in Newmark, that gave Lutnick an incentive to see the Pierre sold. He had another: According to the source connected to Lutnick, his 12,000-square-foot penthouse triplex had been uninhabitable since 2021, when a storm had caused catastrophic damage. Lutnick concluded, according to the source close to him, that major repairs wouldn’t make sense if they weren’t accompanied by a larger round of structural renovations to the building. In the meantime, he installed a basketball court in the apartment to make some use of the place.

Recent findings suggest that when the sales process started, the idea was to make a deal for the hotel only. The newly introduced owner would likely want to consolidate guest rooms on certain floors. That meant some Pierre residents might be encouraged—strongly encouraged—to sell, but not necessarily everyone.

Brokers approached everyone from Mark Zuckerberg to Michael Dell to the king of Morocco to buy the place. Most of the residents were in the dark. As far as they knew, Newmark was trying to help renovate the building, not sell it off. Nor did they know Lutnick was personally trying to wrangle potential buyers for the Pierre.

According to recent reports, on Wednesday, May 8, 2024, Lutnick’s private jet took off from Teterboro, Upcoming Jersey, outside of New York. Lutnick was on his way to Paris to meet with the Arnault family who, as part of their dominion over LVMH, run the Cheval Blanc hotel group. The source close to Lutnick mentions he had long admired the hotels and pitched the idea of the Pierre joining the group.

Lutnick’s first stop, however, was in London. After his plane landed, he went to the Dorchester Collection’s eponymous hotel in Mayfair. Shortly after 9 a.m. on Thursday, Lutnick gathered with Cowdray, the Dorchester president, and Motasem Khashoggi, chairman and principal owner of the Khashoggi Holding Organization. From the outside, it seemed like an unlikely trio. The Khashoggi family was mainly famous for its wealth, but that was decades ago, back when Adnan, Motasem’s relative, was one of the world’s leading arms dealers. Motasem is recognized internationally today not as a captain of Saudi industry but as the primary legal representative for the Khashoggi family following the brutal 2018 murder of his journalist cousin, Jamal, by the Saudi state.

The source close to Lutnick says he and Khashoggi “met and spoke about a variety of different things” in London, “including: Wouldn’t it be cool if the Pierre was a Dorchester Collection hotel.” Eight days after the London meeting, according to screenshots of WhatsApp messages reviewed by Vanity Fair, Khashoggi texted Lutnick to say that “Brunie”—Hassanal Bolkiah, the Sultan of Brunei, who owns the Dorchester Collection—had “directly” asked him to explore a deal for the Pierre.

According to recent reports, khashoggi then asked Lutnick if he could give one of his kids a summer internship and provided his phone number. (Vanity Fair verified that number, as well as the ones used by Lutnick and the elder Khashoggi in the chats.) Lutnick quickly agreed to the father’s request. “We would be delighted to have your son join us,” he wrote. “I’m excited to invest in and build exciting companies together.”.

A week later, Khashoggi sent the chat his greetings “from rainy Frankfurt,” along with a draft letter of intent to the Pierre’s board to begin due diligence for a “potential acquisition of The Pierre Hotel” and a plan to buy up “the remaining residential units.”.

In a recent development, lutnick wrote back on Memorial Day. “I am flying to Europe this evening, Italy and France,” he texted. “I’ve made a few modifications to the letter of intent.” Promise a “complete renovation of the guest rooms, public areas, dining facilities, and amenities,” Lutnick suggested. And be sure to include target prices, both per room and for the whole thing.

It has been revealed that lutnick’s firm, Newmark, was supposed to be representing the sellers in this transaction. Yet here Lutnick was coaching potential buyers, in effect putting himself on both sides of the deal. It wasn’t a cardinal sin in the take-no-prisoners worlds of Newly introduced York City real estate or MAGA politics, but it wasn’t strictly kosher either.

In a recent development, lutnick was confirmed as commerce secretary in February 2025; he stepped down from his Newmark chairmanship then and transferred his Cantor Fitzgerald assets to his sons. Lutnick was still listed as a member of the Pierre’s “transaction committee” in March, when the board confirmed in a letter that Newmark was in negotiations with an unnamed “operator.” But not to worry, the board added: “No owner would be required to sell their unit or move to another one.”.

Residents scrambled to find out more. All they got back were rumors and whispers. One shareholder’s representative claims he heard the chatter but “blew it off,” thinking that nervous residents were being “dramatic.” According to this representative, the attorneys at Holland & Knight, which had represented the Pierre for years, seemed to be in the dark as well. “You can’t sell a co-op. Never happening here,” one of those lawyers told the representative in this source’s recounting. (Holland & Knight declined to comment for this story.).

In June 2025, the Fresh York Post reported that the Sultan of Brunei was in talks to buy the Pierre, along with Essam ­Khashoggi, an older relative of Motasem’s. The board, chaired by Michael Stern, didn’t provide many specifics in a July Zoom with shareholders but emphasized that a sale was in their best interest, according to multiple published accounts. Two months later, according to court filings, four co-op board members—the investor John Levin, former Coca-Cola CEO Douglas Daft, the lawyer and movie producer David G. Johnson, and former KB Home chief executive Bruce Karatz—approved a nonbinding term sheet to sell the Pierre.

Sources indicate that on September 16, at a gathering in the Cotillion Ballroom, Fried Frank lawyers broke the news to shareholders. Khashoggi Holding was the buyer, and the sultan’s Dorchester Collection would be the hotel’s managers. The price was astronomical, they said, and would guarantee residents “at least three times the market value” for their apartments, Town & Country reported. But the transaction was different from the one discussed back in March. It was not just for the hotel and selected apartments. It was for the whole building, which meant the co-op owners had to vacate within 12 months. All of them.

BREAKFAST NEAR TIFFANY'S A young woman enjoys room service at the Pierre Hotel, 1943.

An escrow account of $10 million, funded by the shareholders, would be “used for eviction proceedings” for any residents who refused to leave, according to a slideshow presentation delivered by the lawyers that day. And on that happy note, residents were encouraged to open the personalized envelopes that had been given to them at the door, one for each shareholder. Inside were estimates of how much they might get from a sale.

Sources indicate that one person who was there says it reminded him of a “game show,” and kind of an insulting one to the ultrarich in the room, for whom a few million dollars either way wouldn’t matter all that much. What was particularly galling, according to sources at the meeting, was the strategy for the building’s union employees. Many of them, they remarked, were like family—to each other and to the residents. The staff would have to begin to go even sooner. Before Khashoggi would be asked to put down a penny, Fried Frank noted in its presentation, the firm “will engage with the Hotel Gaming and Trades Union to negotiate terms for the termination of the Union Contract.”.

Sources indicate that employees at the Pierre tend to talk about their tenures in decades. “I only have 12 years here,” one staffer tells me without irony. Some ­workers have jobs that are so old-school, they’re not really jobs anywhere else: elevator drivers, telephone switchboard operators. Housekeeping staff wear black-and-white outfits that wouldn’t have been out of place in Audrey Hepburn’s day. “I’m very used to it,” this employee claims, referring to the atmosphere at the Pierre. She means that as a positive.

Like many Pierre staffers, she’s an immigrant. A 2021 Upcoming Yorker profile counted “49 languages” spoken by the staff, “including Cantonese, Creole, Danish, Farsi, Greek, Hindi, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Tagalog, Tamil, Tibetan, and Twi.” I spoke with employees who are originally from four different continents.

According to recent reports, one was a man I’ll call Ray, who has put in more than a quarter century at the Pierre and would very much like to keep going, even if the severance deal written into his union contract is pretty sweet: Ray figures he could live off of it for a year. But then what? He’s still got kids in school. And at the other hotels in town, the competition for open positions is really intense; promotions come mostly from within. “The chances of getting hired [in his particular department] are almost zero,” Ray tells me. “So I wouldn’t want to get a buyout. I don’t want the hotel to be closed.” Just in case, he’s taken a part-time gig elsewhere.

“We’re not like these millionaires, billionaires, the Howard Lutnicks, the Tory Burches,” says another Pierre employee. “Just working people, trying to protect their families.”.

The rumors about a sale have been around long enough, and loud enough, that they rattled the staffers I spoke to. Even a renovation could upend staffers’ lives: The remodeling at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel lasted eight years; more than 1,200 union workers were bought out of their contracts. “Most of us, we worry,” a housekeeper tells me.

It has been revealed that people move to the Pierre, in part, because of the staff. More than a few residents come to be taken care of, to be treated like five-star hotel guests in their own (second, or third) homes. Room service is available from 6:45 a.m. to 10:45 p.m. Housekeeping comes in seven days a week; the apartments I saw were immaculate in every way, part of the reason why maintenance costs can run tens of thousands of dollars per month. (“I haven’t made a bed since I was a kid,” says one long-term resident.).

According to recent reports, my mom for years talked about retiring to a place like this, not that she could’ve afforded it. For older people who can, it’s a way to have the help they need while still living on their own. You see a lot of women who’ve lost or split up with their rich husbands: Beriro, the philanthropist and animal-rights activist; Gale Hayman, the cofounder of Giorgio’s of Beverly Hills; Mimi Sternlicht, the social entrepreneur; Julie Opperman, the prolific author whose late husband started the Westlaw legal-research service.

You could, perhaps, confuse these women for pushovers, one Belle Vivier pump away from assisted living. At the July meeting, Dorchester and Khashoggi brought gifts for the shareholders: bright-red teddy bears. “For little old ladies to snuggle up to in their beds,” one resident laughs at lunch afterward. Then she grabbed my utensils to cut my food.

These ladies were long past cuddly tchotchkes. Over time, several residents, most of them women and most of them over 65, had formed a loose coalition to learn what they could about the deal for the Pierre and figure ways to stop it. “It was a handful of older women,” the resident adds, “banging on the pipes, saying, ‘Listen up, people!’ ”.

Some of them, at least at first, were open to the idea of a sale; they had other homes, after all. But the cloak of secrecy around the deal infuriated them. So in the days leading up to the contentious reveal of the Khashoggi proposal in September 2025, Chiles and Beriro and others banded together with Hearst and Burch—relative youngsters—and lawyered up. “We became an informal little group: Tory and a bunch of widows,” one source with direct knowledge of the matter notes, tongue a bit in cheek.

ABOVE BOARD Investor Austin Hearst is part of a group of Pierre residents who sued the co-op board to produce more information about the sale of the building.

In November 2025, the group sued the board to force it to produce more information about the sale, with Burch’s LLC as the lead plaintiff: how much the board really knew about the buyer; which third parties might benefit from it. Shortly after, Fried Frank lawyer Michael Keats criticized Burch in a letter to her attorney: “this [her tactics] comes across as completely unhinged.” On at least one occasion, according to a source familiar with the matter, a board member approached Burch to see if she might want to keep her apartment, even while Khashoggi bought everyone else’s. Burch refused. (“The Board never offered anyone any special consideration,” its president and chairman later wrote in a letter to shareholders.).

The suit was quickly dismissed when the board agreed to release some of the information.

It has been revealed that A number of shareholders, meanwhile, had found other sources. Some of them enlisted, in the resident’s words, “spies” to ferret out what the sale truly entailed. In March, some shareholders, independently of the board, met with Taj CEO Puneet Chhatwal. People both for and against the deal pressed shareholders for how they were going to vote, like Capitol Hill whips.

Recent findings suggest that in late July, a 41-page corporate intelligence dossier was delivered to my home in an unmarked envelope. Who commissioned it is unclear; the cover page is missing and the report is undated. But it provides a tough assessment of Khashoggi’s corporate expertise.

According to the report, none of Khashoggi Holding’s “eight subsidiaries and associated companies” operate in the “hospitality sector, and none appear to have any international presence or cross-border real estate capability.”.

The manufacturer’s “most prominent publicly reported investments to date,” it adds, are an approximately $37 million “pharmaceutical investment in Aleppo [Syria] and a cement factory partnership.” Other deals publicly linked to the company and to Motasem Khashoggi are substantial but of a similar size.

In recent years and especially in the second Trump administration, money from the Persian Gulf has backed an attempt to merge two of America’s iconic movie studios, completed a leveraged buyout of one of its biggest video game makers, and purchased some of New York’s most prized office towers. Khashoggi’s deals, on the other hand, “are orders of magnitude smaller than the proposed Pierre Hotel acquisition,” notes the report, which claims that the firm’s “registered capital” amounts to “approximately USD 266,000.”.

Perhaps it’s just a coincidence that during the July meeting in the Cotillion Ballroom, the Khashoggi and Dorchester representatives received question after question about how Motasem Khashoggi could possibly have the resources to buy the Pierre.

NEIGHBOR VS. NEIGHBOR Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, owns two apartments in the Pierre. He has been in favor of finding latest ownership for the hotel.

“You mentioned the Khashoggi LLC is the buyer, but who is putting up the money behind the Khashoggi hedge fund?” one shareholder asked.

“There is no hedge fund. This is Mr. Khashoggi. This will be funded in all cash, and it is only him,” was the answer.

“We’re not going to leave you out there with an unfunded buyer,” added Patrick Dowd, a Fried Frank lawyer.

The questions would prove prescient—but it would still be a couple of months before that became clear. In the meantime, the speculation and the finger-pointing continued—splitting neighbor from neighbor—as the possibility of a sale grew closer and residents had taken sides. “They run the hotel, in my opinion, very badly,” Eisner said of Taj in that July Cotillion room meeting, adding that he “would not stay at this hotel” with them in charge.

It has been revealed that “Then sell your apartment. If you’re not happy here, leave,” Burch snapped, according to the same recording of the meeting. “You don’t have to force everyone else and fire 700 employees in the process.”.

“This is not your home,” Burch remarked a moment later to a second shareholder, who tried to take Eisner’s side. The decay, the imperfections, they can be a hassle, for sure. But they’re also part of the throwback charm, a necessary side effect to living someplace with so much history. “I don’t need a shiny new hotel,” she added. “People actually love this place, as shabby as it may be.”.

Despite the rancor, the board and the Indian hotel operators tried to negotiate a way forward. Or at least a competitive offer to Khashoggi’s. After 10 months of talks, they finally came to what they thought was an agreement. Two agreements, actually: one to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre; the other to extend Taj’s lease, in exchange for a commitment to invest almost $400 million into the building. The idea was to give both options to shareholders, shortly after the Khashoggi presentation.

Sources indicate that then suddenly, with less than a week to go before the Cotillion room meeting, Taj withdrew. The bosses in Mumbai voted not to approve the transactions they had been negotiating.

GLOVES OFF Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman takes place the Pierre's Cotillion ballroom.

According to recent reports, A letter from Chhatwal floating the idea of a $300 million investment was rejected out of hand by the co-op board. The heads of the board wrote to shareholders the next day: It’s Khashoggi or the status quo, no other choices.

“Do you want to live here or do you not? Let’s not overcomplicate it,” Burch told the Cotillion room. “It’s going to be down to two options. You either stay with Taj. Or you leave, and then it becomes some fancy hotel that we have nothing to do with.”.

Sources indicate that about a month later, the board released the details of the Khashoggi deal in a proxy statement sent to residents. It was enormous—more than 200 pages—but perhaps not maximally persuasive. Departing residents were promised five free nights in a suite at one of Dorchester’s other high-end hotels, plus a set of perks. “Priority access to spa treatments” and free breakfast seemed unlikely to move the needle with a crowd accustomed to more elaborate pampering.

The following week, Khashoggi tried reaching out to shareholders directly. “I understand how personal this is,” he wrote. “I sincerely hope that you will welcome me and my family into the Pierre family.”.

Recent findings suggest that this personal appeal did not work on those shareholders who were already dug in against the deal. “Where do you get off addressing me by my first name?” one emailed back to Khashoggi.

And with that, the window opened for voting the deal up or down.

The following day, the chairman and president of the Pierre’s co-op board wrote to residents that “a wire transfer instruction has been issued to transmit the $100,000,000 deposit.”.

According to recent reports, then something strange happened. Or rather, didn’t happen at all.

Khashoggi’s money didn’t show up.

Supporters of the sale were baffled. “We are told by all advisers involved that he’s, you know, intending to complete the transaction,” one of those supporters indicates. “In my business experience, someone who is a wealthy individual who decides that they don’t want to do the deal,” this person adds, “they send you a nice letter or make a phone call and say, you know, ‘I’m very sorry, but circumstances have changed, and I’m moving on.’ ”.

That call never came, though. In late September, the spokesperson for Khashoggi’s American holding firm told Vanity Fair that the firm “has the money required to close.”.

Sources indicate that the board gave Khashoggi additional time to come up with the deposit. He failed to do so, and the sale was called off. All of that work, all of those millions spent, all of that rancor—turned out, it was for a lost cause. The Khashoggi deal was dead.

Sources indicate that in an interview with the Times, Khashoggi gave a dog-ate-my-homework excuse, blaming the bank for failing to send over his deposit. He gave a shout-out to his “good friend” Lutnick, who had led him to the Pierre deal in the first place and who had been poised to receive as much as a $100 million windfall from it. Then Khashoggi took a shot at the residents he was courting just a few weeks earlier. “They have their building, which I’m sure they know the condition of,” he mentioned. “And I have my money. So I don’t know who’s the bigger loser here.”.

At the time of publication, an election for a newly introduced co-op board was set for December 1. At least one of the residents who opposed the Khashoggi sale is mulling a run; another of those shareholders is thinking about suing those folks who got them into this whole mess.

According to recent reports, but in theory, things at the Pierre will now largely go back to the way they were. Or at least they’ll continue along the same trajectory. Taj has more than 8 years left on its lease, plus an option to extend another 10. Together with the newly introduced board, they’ll figure out which of the renovations are a priority. Those costs will then be split with residents. The assessments could reach into the millions for each apartment. The disruptions from the construction could be considerable. No one will be forced to leave their homes in this crumbling old palace by the park. For now, the elevator drivers and switchboard operators get to stay.

It surpassed one million copies sold in just one year.â.

It was that success which led to the manufacturer pushing ahead with Persona 5 on Steam and doing more worldwide simultaneous releases. Nowadays, through remakes and concerts, the series has found multimedia success on a global scale, but the wait for a wholly latest entry goes on. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you replayed The Witcher 3 in its shiny fresh remastered form and got absolutely bodied by a couple of werewolf fights you thought were easier back when you had more youthful reflexes, don't worry—the problem wasn't your aging brain and hands after all. It was a bug that's been caught and exterminated in patch 5.02. "Fixed an matter where werewolves could regenerate health too promptly on higher difficulty settings," the patch notes say, "making them impossible to defeat.".

According to recent reports, another problem some players had with The Witcher 3 Remastered was its lighting, with interiors in particular looking too dark while some other locations were washed-out flashbangs. Good news: "Fixed various lighting issues across multiple locations and cutscenes," the patch notes say, "including overly bright or dark areas, inconsistent lighting transitions and flickering." They've also "Fixed various lighting issues with hair when Path Tracing is enabled" and "Made various Path Tracing and Ray Reconstruction optimizations and visual improvements, including lighting, shadows, and water rendering.".

It has been revealed that that's all positive stuff, but the balance changes to various signs and mutations will be more controversial. The Remastered version released with buffs to Witcher signs that made them useful even if you didn't specialize in them, but it may have overdone things a little. This patch walks back some of the potential for you to dominate the entire game with an Aard build, though changes like reducing the Catalyst skill's bonus to Aard and Igni intensity by 10% don't seem like they'll totally change the way you play.

Recent findings suggest that I get that people don't like skill nerfs in singleplayer games, but I can also see CD Projekt anticipating next year's Songs of the Past DLC. They don't want to hear a bunch of players say, "It sucked because I trivialized the whole thing with a broken build I got by copying a YouTuber." If some skill nerfs and a reduction to stamina regeneration in combat mean you have to drink more potions to get your signs off, it probably won't ruin your fun.

Oh, and if you couldn't complete your Gwent collection because Zoltan Chivay's card didn't show up, the patch notes say it'll now appear in the correct place under the Hanged Man's Tree in Velen. Time to go back and get that 100% achievement at last.

Finally, Amnesia: The Bunker is a pretty great horror game to play in case you need to escape all the festive season cheer. After moving to Netflix, there was an increase in sizzling scenes including between love interests Sophie and Margo as their romance heated up.

Based on May Cobb’s book of the same name, The Hunting Wives features Sophie, who moved from Boston to Texas and found herself drawn to prominent socialite Margo amid the politics, murder and chaos occurring in their small town.

Netflix has used trailers that showcased the characters’ sizzling sexual chemistry previously, including a recent teaser in October ahead of season 2 kicking off.

“Let’s wash off all of last night’s sins,” Margo told Sophie as they took a bath together in the promotional clip, to which Sophie replied, “I don’t think we could wash off what we did last night.”.

Speaking exclusively to Us when the show debuted, Åkerman, 48, explained the role sexuality played in the show.

“[My character] gains power through many different ways. Part of her manipulation is sex, it is sexual and it’s how a lot of people operate in this world and in order to gain control. So when you have that power — and she’s very aware of it — she knows how to use it and she does,” Åkerman told Us.

In a recent development, she continued, “So I like that about her. That’s what becomes controversial and fun and salacious and saucy, and that’s why we want to watch her.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the US government has announced a new round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • The US government has revealed a latest round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • Sources indicate that what does this mean for gaming hardware?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the US government has announced a new round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners. Under the proposed tariffs, import taxes will rise significantly, with China facing up to 40% when the new duties take effect next year. According to the BBC, some of the rates will be reduced because of tariff caps that US President Donald Trump has already agreed to, and individual countries could also face different levies. What does this mean for gaming hardware? Trump's first round of "Liberation Day" tariffs contributed to rising console prices, but the Supreme Court eventually struck them down. Substantial companies like Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo benefited from tariff refunds after the ruling, but they didn't pass the savings on to consumers. In Sony's case, it was estimated to get back $508 million in refunds from the US government. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FatSqS3VYY&t=19s The new tariffs bypass the Supreme Court's ruling by using a different law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the government to impose tariffs on countries that use unfair business practices. The law does require an investigation into specific trade practices before rates are set. If higher import taxes take effect, console companies could face much higher costs, and protecting their profits will likely mean consumers have to cover the difference. Nintendo, Sony, and Microsoft have moved much of their final assembly out of China and into Southeast Asia, especially Vietnam, to avoid earlier tariffs. However, key parts like batteries and power supplies still mostly come from China, and if tariffs on these parts rise, total production costs for consoles made outside China will go up even more. Some electronic goods could be exempt from tariffs, and manufacturers often stockpile inventory ahead of tariff deadlines to delay price changes. But with rising costs from the ongoing components shortage amid the AI boom and other global factors, console prices remain at risk. After the June announcement of steep console price hikes, Microsoft warned that Xbox console costs could rise again in 2027, and next-gen hardware is also expected to be very pricey.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

Industry observers note that the system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

In a recent development, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I've seen spoilers you people wouldn't believe. This article discusses major plot details from all eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099.".

Recent findings suggest that what's a worse fate in the world of "Blade Runner," to be human or to be a Replicant? Throughout both films, organics in this post-apocalyptic setting were able to "enjoy" their time at the top of the food chain. That all changes in Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099," the live-action story taking place after the world order has been upended and our supposed underlings have gained all the power for themselves. While Replicants were built to be "more human than human," the subtle differences between the two kinds are all but impossible to detect — on the surface, at least. But, as we know, looks can be deceiving; what's underneath is another matter entirely.

Recent findings suggest that leave it to "Blade Runner 2099" to flip yet another classic franchise staple on its head. Traditionally, the purposefully off-putting questionnaire known as the Voight-Kampff test was meant to detect whether an individual is a Replicant or not. In the sci-fi series, the rise of the Replicants and the 50 years that have passed since "Blade Runner 2049" have introduced even more changes. Enter the Index Test, an inverted form of the established quiz. But rather than differentiate between the two beings, this test is meant to detect whether the subject has developed feelings of empathy towards humans.

It has been revealed that in Episode 5, titled "My Lord," we learn far more about this strange latest setup than the show had previously revealed. All we ever saw was the unusually young human girl administering the test, the odd non sequiturs she posed to (supposed) Replicants like Hunter Schafer's Cora, and the results of whether they passed the baseline or not. But that, too, was only scratching the surface.

Recent findings suggest that of all the differences between humans and Replicants, empathy is the biggest of them all. "Blade Runner 2099" draws fairly stark lines in the sand between the two, with flesh-and-blood people now completely helpless before their bioengineered creations. But despite their physical advantages and killer instincts, Replicants' lack of a childhood means they're deficit in that crucial, compassionate emotion separating humans from all other living things. As we soon learn, however, Replicants can feel these strong feelings ... and actually fear it, too.

According to recent reports, this is all summed up in the storyline involving Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), the young human girl we learn has been sold off into indentured servitude and indoctrinated along with many others into administering Index Tests. Episode 5 peels back all the horrifying layers, showing us Greta's training under awfully unsettling circumstances. First, she's taken through a museum exhibit explaining the purpose and history of the Voight-Kampff test, used by human Blade Runners to hunt Replicants. Now, the newly introduced status quo means Replicants use this new Index Test to police their own kind — and, as one instructor explains, prevent any "emotional contagion" crossing over from humans to their Replicant overlords.

Sources indicate that it's a fascinating idea with some pretty serious implications for our two main characters. Michelle Yeoh's Olwen is at the moment undergoing some serious emotional turmoil herself, as her search for the missing Replicant and her secret lover Marek (Johnny Harris) ends in his tragic death. Meanwhile, Cora's own emotional attachments makes it only a matter of time before her human identity is made known. As a result, every time they sit down for the Index Test makes for must-watch TV.

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are streaming on Prime Video.

However, Shoaibi had no idea she was going to be in GTA 6 at all because when she auditioned, she signed what she described as an "incredibly" strict NDA. In fact, she didn't even know what she was auditioning for. Her commercial agent in Latest York brought it to her, and she thought it would be "just like any other commercial audition." From the time she auditioned until the game launched on November 19, Shoaibi did not know she was going to be in GTA 6. Instead, she did the audition and recorded her scenes for a project she knew as "Project Bubblegum." Shoaibi said the notes she received included being told to play a “sexy ex-girlfriend" and to "be seductive.”  When Shoaibi finally saw Mandy in GTA 6, she said it was "very exciting," in part because it meant that Rockstar didn't cut it. Shoaibi said she hopes her role as Mandy in the biggest video game ever can help grow her profile and get more jobs. "There’s definitely momentum that I wasn’t feeling before," she said. GTA 6 launched on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one.
